summary: The Wealth Tax Officer included a sum of Rs. 1,50,000 estimated as the accrued interest on the assessee 's money lending investments. The assessee assessee was assessed to wealth tax for the assessment years 1965 66, 1966 66 and 1967 66. The Wealth Tax Appellate Tribunal held that the assessee was liable to be included in the wealth tax assessments of the assessee. The Appellate Tribunal, however, rejected the claim of the Appellate Assistant Commissioner. The High Court, in a reference under section 27 of the Wealth Tax Act, dismissed the appeals. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: (1) Under section 3 of the Income Tax Act the net wealth of an assessee has to be determined as it obtains on a particular date. It is the estimated open open market value of the rights in the property which constitute the asset. If the asset is an asset other than cash, its value is determined pursuant to sub section (I) of section 7 as the estimated price, which, in the opinion of the Sales Tax Officer, the asset would fetch if sold in the open market on the valuation date. In other words, it would be the estimated of the assets in the assets of the appellant during that period. That being so, the conclusion is inescapable that even though the accounts of the Revenue assessee are maintained on cash basis interest due on accrual basis, though not realised, on the outstandings of the money lending business are liable to he included in their wealth. [5D E] (2) The assets are not confined to cash. Where the asset was an assets other than the asset, it is immaterial whether the assessee employs one system of accounting or another. There is clear indication that the assets to be considered are not circumscribed by any consideration of the particular system of assessment adopted by the assessee; and that what accrues as a right also falls to be mentioned within the assets. [6D] (3) In the instant case, there is an apparent advantage in adopting as the valuation day the last day of a period which is also the relevant period under the Income tax Act. [7D]

The High Court held that the respondent was guilty of entering the name of the first respondent in the pay roll for May 1969 and that he should not be dismissed or removed by an authority subordinate to that by which he was appointed. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Tribunal had no power to interfere with the punishment imposed by the disciplinary authority. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The jurisdiction of the Tribunal to interfere under the disciplinary matters or punishment cannot be equated with an appellate court. The Tribunal is not concerned to decide whether the penalty imposed is justified by the rules, is appropriate having regard to the gravity of misdemeanour for which the punishment can lawfully be imposed, it is not for the Court to consider whether that ground alone would have weighed with the authority in dismissing the public servant. [631E F] 2.2 The power to impose penalty on a delinquent officer is conferred on the competent authority either by an Act of legislature or rules made under the proviso to Article 309 of the constitution of the tribunal. The High Court dismissed the second respondent 's suit holding that the suit was barred by the principle of res judicata and that the civil court had no jurisdiction to try the same merely because of the subsequent change in law. The petitioners are carpenters and are given all benefits due to them under the various labour legislations. The Government has not fixed the wage scale payable to the petitioners engaged in the Development industry. They are paid the same wages as are payable to carpeners, painters and carpesters. The petitioners are paid all the same pay of their counterparts in the Government service. Their claim for parity of pay for equal work is based on the allegations that he was performing the same duties and performing similar functions as "Senior Physi cents". The petitioners claim that the unit where the petition is working is a factory registered under the Factories Act, and that the Corporation has adopted the minimum wages payable for similar work in the construction industry and they are being paid the maximum wages prescribed by the Deputy Commissioner for like categories of workmen. Dismissing the writ petition, the Court, HELD: 1.1 The principle of equal pay in the same cadre on the basis of selection based on merit with due regard to experience and seniority. It is open to the State to classify employees on the principle of qualifications, duties and responsibilities of the posts concerned. If the classification has reasonable nexus with the object sought to be achieved, efficiency in the administration, the State would be justified in prescribing different pay scales. [667G H] 1.2 The principle relating to equal pay is not one of the fundamental rights expressly guaranteed by the Constitution. The principle has to be read into Article 14 of the Constitution which enjoins the State not to deny any person equality before the law or the equal protection of the same right. The classification cannot be in every kind of service particularly in the area of professional services. It must be left to be evaluated and determined by expert body. The accuracy required by the job and the dexerity it affords may differ from job to job. It cannot be evaluated by the mere averments in the self serving affidavits or counter affidavits of the parties. It has not been extended to employees of the Corporation. The Court, therefore, cannot direct the Corporation to apply the rates prescribed under exhibit P. 2 unless the Government makes it applicable to the employees of Corporation. Section 3 of the Andhra Pradesh General Sales Tax Act, 1957, provides that "cinematograph equipment, including cameras, projectors, and sound recording and reproducing equipment shall be required for use as parts and accessories of motor vehicles". The appellants were, therefore, compelled to consider the use of the word "Cinematograph" to them because of the use to which they were generally put. The Sales Tax Appellate Tribunal allowed an application for adducing expert evidence to determine the question whether are carbons manufactured by the appellant company could be covered by the entry in the 1st Schedule to the Act. Dismissing the appeal to this Court, ^ HELD: (1) The High Court rightly held that the appellants were not entitled to be produced their account books to show that they had been purchased by persons other than those who went cents or for any other use. The fact that they can also be used for search clothes, signalling, stage lighting, or where powerful lighting or other purposes may be required, could not detract from the classification to which the carbon controller belongs. [618 C D] (2) The expression "accessories" is used in the schedule to describe goods which may have been manufactured for use, as an aid or addition. The same item may be an accessory of something else. A sense in which the word access is used is given in Webster 's Third International Dictionary as follows: "all objects or purpose that is not essential in itself but that adds to the beauty, convenience, or effectiveness of anything else else. [718 C E] (3) In the instant case, the High Court was in error in holding that the main use was duly proved to be that of production of powerful light used in projectors in cinematographs. The finding was enough, however, to justify the view taken by the State, that the goods under consideration were covered under the relevant entry No. 4. [818 D E] State of Andhra Pradesh vs The State of Mysore, ; , referred to. (4)The High Court had held that there was no substance in the very different entry in a schedule of an entirely different Act of a different State. [519 C] (5) The State 's contention was that the primary or ordinary use or ordinary to something else was used for equipment or accessories connected with the main purpose, and that it was determined by their ordinary or commonly known purpose or user.

The petitioners challenged the validity of a notification issued by the Government of Gujarat on June 26, 1985 in exercise of its powers conferred by section 15 of the Act. The validity of the notification dated June 18, 1981 under which the rate of royalty had been raised was upheld and the writ petitions in which the validity had been challenged were dismissed by the High Court. The petitioners contended that (i) the royalty levied and covered under the Rules should be applied only for mineral development and (ii) the impugned notification in question was in contravention of clause (b) of Article 304 of the Constitution. Dismissing the petitions, this Court, HELD: (1) The Act is passed for devel ment of minerals, but while discharging its functions relating to development, if the State incidentally allows mining to be carried on in the public interest and levies in that connection a tax, it does not mean that the said tax should be used only for development of minerals and not for other purposes sanctioned by law. The Act does not authorise the State Government to show such concession while promulgating the Rules which are in the nature of sub holderi nate legislation is also of no consequence. [594F G] (2) The levy of royalty in the State of Rajasthan on the minor minerals would be bad in law and liable to be struck down by the courts but the possibility of abuse of power cannot invalidate the statute con privting the power or the power which has been conferred by it. The appellant was elected as a trustee by the Maharaja. According to the appellant the temple was rounded two hundred years ago by the members of his community and since then the management of the temple and is affairs was always vested in the community of the deceased, the appellant was declared to be a trustee under the provisions of Madras Act 1 of 1951. The appellant 's case was that the trusteeship was not hereditary. The High Court, in appeal, set aside the judgment of the High Court. In appeal to this Court, HELD: The word "regulated by usage" in section 6(9) of the Madras Act must be construed along with the word "recommunity to this office" and when so construed that part of the definition would only apply where the ordinary rules of succession under the Hindu law are modified by usage and succession has to be determined in accordance with the modified rules. The expression "regified by usage", in relation to property and rights and interests in property generally implies "passing of an interest from one person to another" (vide section 6) and the definition of the trustee is identical in both the Acts. The definition of hereditary trustee in section 4(9), must be interpreted along with, the expression "resulated by the founder" and, when so interpreted, it is possible that for that vacancy a himself might be reelected because a retiring trustee is eligible for reelection. The possibility of the appellant being the successor A himself is not merely an anomaly, but the right of the latter should not depend upon the choice of any individual. [5 D E] State of Madras vs Krishna, ; , referred to.

The appellant who was a postman attached to the Kendriya Post Office was tried for offences under section 52 of the Indian Post Office Act, 1898, and in two of them for offence under sections 468 and 471 of the Penal Code. The Additional Sessions judge acquitted the appellant but reduced the appeal to the High Court. The State appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave. The appellant contended that (i) the search was illegal inasmuch as it was in contravention of the provisions of sections 52 and 161 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898; (ii) the seizure was illegal; (iii) it was not proved that the five registered letters were in the exclusive possession of the appellant; and (iv) the appellant was in possession of two rooms only. Held, that the appellant had failed to prove that these documents were forged but had failed before the Court of Sessions and the Government not having appealed against that part of the decision of the Court, it must be held that there were compelling reasons for setting aside the appellant 's acquittal without coming to the conclusion that there was sufficient reasons for doing so. In so far as the contravention of section 342 of the Act is concerned it is sufficient to say that no grievance was made either before the court of the Additional Sessions Judge or before a High Court that there had been such a contravention and the appellant could not be said to have violated the letter.

The appellants were convicted for contempt of court and sentenced to pay a fine of Rs. 1,000/ . The High Court, on appeal, held that the appellants had disobeyed an order of stay passed by the High Court. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) It is true that in certain cases proceedings can be adjourned to enable the parties to file better proof, but a judicial officer is not bound to do so and, if he bona fide does not in his discretion adjourn proceedings, it cannot be said that he has committed contempt of Court for disobeying the order. It must also be borne in mind that the witnesses are not well versed in law and procedure and the records maintained by them should not be judged in the same manner as that of ordinary courts. In such matters those who assert that a person had knowledge of the order must prove this fact beyond all reasonable doubt. If a person bona fide comes to the conclusion on the material placed before him that the source of information is not authentic, he cannot be held guilty of contempt of the court for contravening its orders unless there is unimpeachable evidence that the judicial officer had knowledge that the order was passed deliberately to by pass the order and if he was present in court when the order of the High court had already stayed the proceedings for a short while and should have asked the applicant to produce a certified copy of the stay order. The order or order should be served on the party personally, except in the following cases : (1) prohibitive orders, the drawing up of which is not completed; and (2) in such matters, those who allege that the person has knowledge of that order must establish this fact within all reasonable doubts. If there is any doubt, the benefit ought to be given to the person charged with contempt of a court. If it is proved that the advantage ought to have been given to him to the accused, it must be clearly proved that it was not signed by the party to the order, and the application seems to be made after the proceedings on that date had commenced and evidence taken. It was contended on behalf of the respondents that (i) the State of West Pakistan, and (ii) the whole of section 5 (1) could not be regarded as discriminatory as being opposed to equality before the law and the equal protection of the laws guaranteed by article 14 of the Constitution of India; (iii) the classification implied in article 14 was not violative of article 14; and (iv) the impugned Act was invalid as it was violative of Article 14. Held, (per Hidayatullah, C.J., dissenting) that the power to direct "cases" as distinct from "classes of offences" to be tried by a Special court under article 226 of the constitution must be a valid one, as not having a relation to the object to be attained, or is concerned only with the grouping of "physical" and "arbitrary" the fact that the whole object and purpose of the legislation was to devise machinery for "porter trial of certain offences" and the charge of discriminatory treatment must fail. The State Government had no power to classify either in the adoption of police laws, or tax laws, nor was it a minor offence within the meaning of the section. The power to deal with a particular situation within the general rule prescribed by the Act must be based on some intelligible differentia which should have a reason able relation to that object and the object of the statute, for, in the absence of any special circumstances, there is no nexus between the two alleged offenders and the intention of the legislature and the legislature; and even if any unguided power has been conferred on the executive, the Act itself cannot be said to have violated the equality clause, though it is a key to the understanding of the enactment and the effect of the repugnancy of the law.

The appellant, who was the predecessor in interest of the appellant, filed a suit for recovery of certain movable property in respect of the land of the respondents ' coal land. The suit was decreed by the Subordinate Judge. The Subordinate Judge held that the suit was barred by limitation and that the appellant had failed to prove that the respondents had knowledge of the said encroachment only within three years of the date of the filing of the suit. On appeal the High Court held that article 48 of the Limitation Act was applicable to the suit and that it was not permissible for a court to reconstruct the plan with reference to revenue records when the plan was self contained and drawn to scale and incorporated in the lease deed, and that in view of the fact that the land in question belonged to the respondents, the respondents could request the mining authorities to exempt them from the operation of rule 76 of the Indian Coal Mines Regulation, 1946, and if exemption was granted, they could remove the coal left by the appellant in the acquired area. Held, that the finding of fact on the assumption that the initial burden of proof to establish knowledge on the part of the respondent beyond the prescribed time was not correct. The High Court was right in holding that the respondent 's right to establish that the knowledge of his father 's possession was not barred by the limitation, it was open to the court to take an inference that if a person has a right to sue within four years from the date when the person having the right to the possession of the property, the suit is within time. It is the duty of the plaintiff to satisfy the court that his action is not barred under the lapse of time. The burden to prove in the sense of adducing evidence shifts from time to time having regard to the evidence adduced by one party or the presumption of fact or law raised in favour of one or the other. In the present case, the burden of proving the knowledge was on the respondents. The courts were, therefore, right in accepting the findings of the courts below on mere probabilities without clear evidence to sustain them.

The appellant 's appeal to the Industrial Tribunal was dismissed. The respondent 's writ petition was dismissed by the Industrial Court. Held, that the Industrial Tribunals had the right to inquire into the causes that might have led to termination of service of an employee and that the employer was empowered to take action under the terms of the contract of employment. The employer could not be said to have acted under the conditions of the contractual provisions. The industrial adjudication by the Government of Kerala in the present case had no application to the facts of this case because, in the circumstances it could not come to the conclusion that the order of discharge was mala fide or was a result of victimisation or unfair labour practice.

The assessee, a partner of a business firm, was carrying on business as grain tillers. The assessee had a substantial credit balance of Rs.50,000 to his son and his son. The income of the assessee was Rs.60,000 and the assessee claimed to have gifted the said amounts by transfer entries in the books of the firm. The Income Tax Officer and the Appellate Assistant Commissioner rejected the assessee 's appeal on the ground that he made a gift of the value of the property in question. The High Court, in appeal, affirmed the decision of the High Court. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that the gift evidenced by the entries in his own account and by the declaration, did not operate to bring into existence a valid gift. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) In case of gift of immovable property, the transfer may be effected by a registered instrument signed by the donor and attested or by delivery. Such delivery may be made in the same way as goods sold may be delivered. The firm in which the donor may have account may or may not have sufficient cash balance but it must have sufficient provision for overdraft with the bank on the basis of which it would reputation in structions given by the assessee. [528B C] (2) In the instant case, there was no valid gift on the date of the entries, then it could not be said that, subsequently, when the money was transferred by further entry entries, it resulted in a valid transfer. [628C] (3) In cases of non banking companies or other firms, if these companies or firms do not have overdraft facilities, it is not possible to make valid gift if sums or funds are not available. The circumstances must be such as to make it clear that there were sufficient funds at the disposal of the donor by reason of which he could make the gift by debiting his account and crediting the account in the name of the donee. But in such cases, merely books entries would not be sufficient to constitute valid gift, but where a sum was not available with the firm or a company which was not a banking company or which had no overdraft facility, by mere book entries even though there was acceptance of that gift by the donor would not effectuate a valid dona tion. In such cases merely books of account would not constitute delivery of possession over the gifted property to the doner and gift in such a case will not be valid.

The appellants contended that the provisions of the Act and the Rules framed thereunder constitute an unreasonable restriction upon the appellants ' fundamental right to do business and that they not only do not achieve the object for which they are enacted but defeat their purpose. Held, that the impugned provisions of section 5(4) of that Act constitute reasonable restriction upon a citizen 's right to carry on the business of selling or selling any commercial crop or crops and the sale of such agricultural crops or trees in a particular area and the notification directing the constitution of a market in the same locality, when admittedly the entire scheme of building a net work of markets could not be completed within a reasonable distance from the market as may from time to time be fixed by the State Legislature and that nothing under the Act prevents the Government from fixing a long distance as a prohibited area. The Act, therefore, was not a valid provision for the exemption of trade allowance and did not operate upon any other payments made which were not trade allowances. It is not necessary to express any opinion on the question whether the right of the appellants falls under article 19 (1)(f) or under both the sub clauses, (g), (h) or (i) of section 2(1) or section 5 prohibits the deduction of trade allowances and does not operate as a trade allowance prescribed by the bye laws framed under that Act. It depends upon the conditions of obtaining in the trade in commercial crops, the standards that will be maintained in the present market at that time, the comparative merits of the existing market and the market to be built up and other relevant considerations which cannot now be visualised. The circumstances in one case cannot be used as a precedent to determine the conclusion on the facts in another case. In the present case, there is no charge under section 149 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and the conviction of the appellants under section 304 of the Penal Code is therefore justified. The conviction under section 307 of the I.P.C. is set aside.

The appellants applied for an interim injunction restraining the Bank of India Ltd. to take any steps in pursuance of a letter of credit opened in favour of M/s. V/s L/O L/W/T/T. The appellants applied to the suit for interim injunction against the Bank. The suit was dismissed by the trial court. In appeal, the High Court held that the appeal was not maintainable since the decision on the issue did not finally dispose of the dispute between the parties. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the order granting interim injunction was not a final order within the meaning of article 134(1)(a) of the Constitution; and (ii) the appeal should be dismissed. HELD: (1) The order refusing to grant interim injunction did not determine the rights and obligations of the parties in relation to the matter in dispute in the suit. The expression "final order" in article 133(1) in the context in which it occurs means a final adjudication by the Court of the rights of the party, and that an interlocutory judgment even if it decides an issue or issues without finally determining the rights or liabilities of the Parties is not a judgment, however cardinal the issue may be. [5 B C] (2) In the present case not even an issue has been decided and the appellants may have to seek amendment of the plaint to get effective relief, an order which is essentially an interlocutory order may be deemed final for the purposes of article 132(1). [6 B] (3) The expression 'final order ' has been used in contradistinction to what is known as "interlocutory order" and an interim order even if the order is made, the order will certainly be a final one, but if the suit is still left alive and has got to be tried in the ordinary way, no finality could attach to the order. [6 D E] (4) The word "speaking order ' in article 134 (1 ) in the sense in which the word occurs means an order, decree or final order. If the decision is not finally disposed of, and the suit or proceeding was a living one, yet to be heard and the rights in disputes have to be determined, the Order is not final. [7 C D]

The appellant was appointed as a Head Clerk on June 1, 1963, long before the Amending Act came into force on June 13, 1973. He was confirmed in that post in course of time. On January 21, 1973 a resolution was passed by respondent No. 3 regularising the post of Head Clerk. The appellant was promoted as Head Clerk with effect from January 1, 1974. The Punjab Panchayat Samitis (Haryana Amendment) Act, 1973 introduced extensive amendments in the Act of 1961. Section 33(1) of the Act provides that persons employed by a Panchayat Samiti before April 1, 1973 and who were in service at the commencement of the Amending Amendment Act shall continue to service on the same terms and conditions on which they were employed by the Panchayat Samiti from time to time. In pursuance of this provision of section 14(4) the appellant was entitled to be absorbed in Government service as a head Clerk in any event. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In the appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that by reason of the amendment of section 33(4), the appellant had been entitled to continue in the service of the Panchayat Parishad in view of the fact that such appointment was made after May 13, 1974 when the Amending Ordinance came into operation. Dismissing the appeal, the Court, ^ HELD: 1. The order of the High Court cannot be sustained. Even assuming for the purposes of argument that the right to be considered for promotion is a term and condition of service, what is relevant for our purpose is not whether the appellant is entitled to he considered for appointment but, whether the Panchayat Panchayat had the right of appointment to the post. he was appointed lawfully to the posts of a Head clerk. [722C D] 2. The fact that the appellant, according to the terms and terms of his service with the Panchayats, was not whether it purported to do, in January 1974 on an ad hoc basis or in April 1974 on a regular basis. The appointment of a appellant to a post being without the authority of law, the Government was not bound to absorb him in the post and that is the post in which the Government had absorbed him. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) It must be a rational relation between the sum so paid and its potential as provision for maintenance. To interpret otherwise is to stultify the project. Law is dynamic and its meaning must be to obviate destitution of the divorcee and to provide her with where withal to maintain herself. The whole scheme of section 127(3) is manifestly to recognise the substitute maintenance arrangement by lump sum payment organised by the custom of the community or the personal law of the parties. The only just construction of the section is that Parliament intended divorcees should not derive a double benefit. If the first payment by way of inheritance has a reasonable relation to the object and is a capitalised substitute for the order under section 125, not mathematically but fairly then section 125 (3) subserves the goal and repatriating the marriagee. [20A B] (2) In the normal course, an order for maintenance must follow, the quantum having been determined by the learned Magistrate at the trial level. [22 E G] (4) The appeal must be allowed and the order of the trial court restored.

The respondent landlord filed a suit for recovery of arrears of rent on the basis of the fair rent fixed by the Rent Controller under section 4(5) of the Madras City Tenants ' Protection Act, 1948. The Rent Controller decreed the suit on the ground of non bona fide denial of title to the appellant. The appellant filed a revision petition in the High Court against the order of the Court of Small Causes. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) since the subject matter of the lease under exhibit P 1 was only a vacant piece of land, and (ii) the Rent Control Act, 1944, had not been fulfilled; and (iii) the respondent landlord had no jurisdiction to determine the question as to whether the premises were at one time let out as a whole and then let out in parts as contended by the respondents. Dismissing the appeal, the Court, HELD: (1) Under section 10(1) (vii) and (2) (viii) and section 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the question on which the jurisdiction of the civil court is excluded is only the determination as to the proper rent of the premises.
